title: Reliable Integrations And Customer Workflows Checkpoint

questions.prompt: A remote action may have succeeded before the response timed out. What is the next safe design step?

options.label: Retry with a new operation key until a success response arrives.
Mark it failed and forget that the remote effect may exist.
Reconcile using the original operation identity or provider-supported idempotency.

questions.explanation: A lost response creates uncertainty. A new key may repeat the action, while forgetting the uncertainty prevents correct recovery.

questions.prompt: Tenant A and tenant B both use request key k1. What identity does the lesson reducer use?

options.label: Only the payload because identical inputs always mean the same intent.
The pair of authenticated tenant and request key.
Only k1 because request keys are always globally unique.

questions.explanation: The fixture scopes keys by authenticated tenant. Payload equality does not determine intent and unscoped keys mix customers.

questions.prompt: A job is saved but the process crashes before queue publication. Which mechanism preserves dispatch intent?

options.label: Write the job and an outbox record in one durable transaction.
Keep the publish intent only in a local variable.
Assume provider idempotency also fixes the database-to-queue gap.

questions.explanation: The outbox closes the local acceptance/publication gap. Memory is lost on crash; provider idempotency addresses repeated remote effects, a different boundary.

questions.prompt: A connector receives repeated transient failures. Which retry policy is defensible?

options.label: Retry immediately forever with unlimited concurrent requests.
Retry every authorization failure as if it were transient.
Bound attempts and total time, back off with jitter, and respect provider guidance.

questions.explanation: Bounded retries control load and time. Unlimited attempts amplify failure, while persistent authorization errors require a different response.
